deep.reconstruction:
Folio 6r has no formulas, numbers or words by Gauss. The only text is archival: the shelfmark 'Math 33', the folio number '6.', an old foliation '154' struck through and replaced by '132', and a later librarian's dating '[Nach 1831 : III Z]'. So there is no derivation to reconstruct. What follows describes the drawing and gives cautious hypotheses.

DESCRIPTION. The figure is ink on squared paper and is mirror-symmetric about a vertical segment.
- The vertical segment has a small circle at its upper end and a small cross ('x') at its midpoint.
- Just to the right is a second, fainter vertical stroke. It is apparently pencil, perhaps a construction line or an aborted redraw.
- Two isolated dots lie on the horizontal through the midpoint mark, one on each side of the axis at equal distance.
- On each side of the axis is one curve branch. Taking the left one: it starts far out at the upper left and descends with increasing slope to a sharp corner or cusp at its lowest point. That corner is marked with a small circle and has faint pencil strokes radiating from it, which look like tangent or continuation directions. From there it rises to the right, turns smoothly through a vertex nearest the axis, at roughly the height of the dots, and heads up and to the left. The branch is thus open, convex toward the axis, with one non-smooth point. The right branch mirrors it, but its corner carries no circle.
- The left branch also bears a small tick near its upper-left end and two pinpoint dots along its lower arc. These are probably plotted points through which the curve was drawn.
- The dark blot at the right is paper damage or ink, not mathematics.

CONTEXT (previous page, my verification). The table there tabulates a single quartic. With f(z)=3z^4+2z^3-3z^2+3, the real column fits f(n) for n=-3..3 exactly (165, 23, 1, 3, 5, 55, 273). The complex column is f(n+i):
- n=0: f(i)=9-2i.
- n=3: f(3+i)=99+322i.
- n=-3: f(-3+i)=27-218i.
- n=±2: the imaginary parts agree (+82, -38), but the real parts compute to -23 and -31, whereas the table has -17 and -25.
The same page draws nested closed curves with double points (figure-eights inside ovals). These are typical of level curves |f(z)|=const, or of the curves Re f=0 and Im f=0. Gauss used such curves in his topological proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra (1799, 1849).

HYPOTHESES for this figure (none certain):
(a) It continues that study: plotted points, with the corner being a point where two branches of a level curve cross and only one half is inked. The pencil rays at the corner support this. But the critical points of this particular f are all real (z=0, 1/2, -1). The figure would then need the real axis drawn vertically, and the corners do not sit at those points. So the link to that specific quartic is doubtful.
(b) It is a genuine cusped curve, such as a caustic or evolute-type curve. The evolute of a hyperbola, (a x)^(2/3)-(b y)^(2/3)=(a^2+b^2)^(2/3), has two mirror-image cusped branches. But its cusps lie on the symmetry line through the centre, which does not match the drawing.
Neither identification can be confirmed from the page.
errors: No mathematical steps on this page to check.

Context, previous page: if f(z)=3z^4+2z^3-3z^2+3 is the tabulated function (it fits five of seven complex entries and all seven real ones exactly), then the entries for 2+i and -2+i should have real parts -23 and -31, not -17 and -25. This is either a slip by Gauss (a consistent +6 error at n=±2) or a transcription error.

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only an unlabeled sketch with no text or formulas. Nothing on it can be attributed as a result. At most it belongs to Gauss's well-known work on curves associated with polynomials.

transcription_corrections: The old foliation reads '154' struck through, then '/ 132'. The first number is cancelled, not bracketed.
'[Nach 1831 : III Z]' is a later archival dating and classification, not Gauss's hand.
The small circle at a cusp appears only at the LEFT branch's corner; the right corner is unmarked. Faint pencil rays emanate from the left corner.
The midpoint mark on the vertical axis is a small cross 'x'. The axis has a small circle at its top end only.
The second vertical line right of the axis is fainter (pencil or diluted ink) and shorter.
There are additional pinpoint dots and a small tick along the left branch (plotted points). The dark spot at the right margin is a stain or damage, not part of the figure.
